Partitioned Distributed Commit Log Broker

A distributed event backbone built around append-only ordered partitions, producer and consumer workflows, offset tracking, and leader-follower replication.

SOURCE PAGE 1 / 14

This report evaluates the feasibility of designing and building a partitioned distributed commit log broker: a messaging system, in the family of Apache Kafka, Redpanda and Apache Pulsar, that stores events in append-only, ordered logs (partitions) spread across multiple servers (brokers). Producers append records, consumers read them by tracking offsets, and replication between a leader and its followers keeps data safe when a machine fails.

Problem. Applications made of many services (orders, payments, inventory, email, analytics) become fragile when services call each other directly. A failure or slowdown in one service spreads to the others, adding a new consumer means changing producer code, and events are lost when a receiver is down. A durable, replayable, horizontally scalable event backbone removes these problems.

Key findings.

• Technically feasible. Every core mechanism (append-only segment files, offset indexes,

hash partitioning, consumer groups, leader-follower replication) is well documented and can be built with commodity tools in Python, Java or Go. A single-broker prototype is low risk, and a multi-broker replicated prototype is moderate risk. • Economically feasible. The prototype can be developed and demonstrated on a laptop

at essentially zero cost. A small three-node cloud demo cluster costs a modest amount per month (see Section 6). • Operationally feasible with conditions. Running a self-built broker in production is not

recommended. Operating a distributed log safely demands expertise, monitoring and tooling that mature products already provide. • Schedule feasible. A phased delivery of 6 to 8 weeks fits a typical microproject window

if scope is controlled. • Compliance manageable. Immutable logs conflict with data-erasure rights unless

retention and encryption controls are designed in from the start.

Recommendation: GO, as a phased design-and-prototype project (Option C, Levels 1 to 3 committed, Level 4 optional). For any real production workload, the recommendation is to adopt an existing platform (Option B) and use this project's design as the reference architecture for understanding and tuning it.

2. Problem Statement and Scope

2.1 Context and current limitations

Consider a typical shopping application where the Order service must trigger an email, an inventory update, a delivery request, an analytics update and a fraud check.

Pain point in the direct-call design Consequence

Tight coupling between caller and every receiver

Adding or removing a service requires changing and redeploying the caller

Synchronous dependency chain One slow or failed service can fail the whole order

No buffering Traffic spikes overwhelm slow services

No durable history Events missed during a crash are gone, and new services cannot backfill past events

Weak ordering guarantees Updates for the same customer may be processed out of order

2.2 Objectives

1. Decouple producers from consumers through a durable broker. 2. Provide high write and read throughput through partitioning. 3. Guarantee ordering within a partition (and therefore per key). 4. Survive single-broker failure with no loss of committed data. 5. Allow independent consumers and replay of historical events. 6. Support horizontal scaling by adding brokers and partitions.

2.3 Scope

In scope

• Topics, partitions, producers, consumers, consumer groups, committed offsets • Append-only segmented storage with offset index and time or size based retention • Leader-follower replication with an in-sync replica (ISR) set and high watermark • Configurable acknowledgment levels (acks=0, 1, all) • Controller for metadata, heartbeats and leader election • At-least-once delivery semantics

Out of scope (future work)

• Exactly-once transactions • Log compaction

2.4 Requirements summary

Type Requirement

Functional Create topic with N partitions; produce with optional key; consume from an offset; consumer groups with partition assignment; commit and fetch offsets

Non-functional High throughput, durability of committed records, fault tolerance for one broker failure, ordering per partition, horizontal scalability, observability (basic metrics)

3. Proposed Design Alternatives

Three approaches were evaluated against the objectives above.

Option A: Traditional message queue (RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ style)

A central broker holds queues. A message is delivered to one consumer and then deleted after acknowledgment.

• Strengths: Simple mental model, mature tooling, excellent for task distribution and

flexible routing. • Weaknesses: Messages are removed after consumption, so replay is not natural. Several

independent readers need duplicated queues. Scaling a single queue across machines is limited. Throughput is lower than log-based systems at large scale.

Option B: Adopt an existing distributed log platform (Kafka, Redpanda, managed cloud service)

Use a proven product, either self-hosted or as a managed service, and design only the producer and consumer applications.

• Strengths: Production-hardened, large ecosystem (connectors, monitoring, client

libraries), strong community, no need to engineer the broker. • Weaknesses: Little learning of internals, operational complexity if self-hosted, recurring

cost if managed, possible vendor lock-in to a cloud provider's variant.

Option C: Design and prototype a custom partitioned commit log broker (proposed)

Design the full architecture and build a layered prototype that implements the core mechanisms.

• Strengths: Deep understanding of partitioning, replication, storage and delivery

semantics. Full control over scope. Ideal for a system design microproject. Produces a reference architecture and a working demonstration. • Weaknesses: Not production-ready. Subtle distributed-systems bugs (split brain, replica

divergence, rebalancing storms) are easy to introduce. Performance will be well below mature products.

Conclusion of the comparison. For delivering a real business workload, Option B wins. For a system design microproject whose purpose is to design, justify and demonstrate the architecture, Option C wins. The recommendation therefore treats them as complementary: build Option C to learn and demonstrate, adopt Option B for production.

4. Technical Feasibility

4.1 Proposed architecture (summary)

• Producers send records (key, value, timestamp) to a topic. The partition is chosen as

hash(key) % partition_count, or round-robin when no key is given. • Brokers store partitions as sequences of segment files (.log plus .index). Only the

active segment is written, and older segments are read-only and deleted whole by retention. • Replication: each partition has one leader and several followers. Followers fetch from

the leader. A record is committed once all in-sync replicas have it, and consumers may read only up to the high watermark. • Controller tracks broker liveness via heartbeats, stores metadata (topics, partitions,

leaders, ISR) and elects a new leader from the ISR on failure. In a production design this is a Raft quorum. In the prototype it can be a single controller process. • Consumer groups: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group.

Committed offsets are stored per group, topic and partition. Membership changes trigger rebalancing.

4.5 Performance expectation

The design principles that make mature log systems fast are all reproducible in a prototype: sequential appends, batching, reliance on the operating system page cache, and avoiding unnecessary copies. A well-written prototype can be expected to reach thousands to tens of thousands of messages per second on a laptop (depending on language and batching), which is sufficient to demonstrate partition parallelism and the effect of acks settings. It will not match mature products, and the report should not claim that it does. Actual numbers must be measured and reported honestly.

4.6 Technical feasibility verdict

Feasible. Levels 1 to 3 are low to moderate risk. Level 4 (replication and failover) is achievable with a simplified controller, and it should be scheduled with a time buffer.

5. Operational Feasibility

5.1 Fit with existing workflows

The broker exposes a small, familiar API (produce, consume, commit offset). Services only need a thin client library, and producers and consumers can be adopted one at a time. Existing synchronous flows can be migrated gradually: first publish events in parallel with existing calls, then switch consumers over once they are verified.

5.2 Adoption and user impact

Stakeholder Impact Adoption concern

Developers of producing services

Replace direct calls with a publish call

Must learn keys, partitioning and idempotency

Developers of consuming services

Poll loop, offset management

Must write idempotent handlers (at- least-once delivery)

Operations or demo owner

Start, stop and monitor brokers

Needs runbooks and basic dashboards

Evaluators or reviewers Understand and assess the design

Needs clear diagrams and documentation

5.3 Support and maintenance

• Monitoring needs: consumer lag per group and partition, under-replicated partitions,

ISR size, disk usage, broker liveness. • Routine operations: adding brokers, increasing partitions, adjusting retention, rotating

segments.

• Operational burden: distributed logs require capacity planning (disk and network),

careful partition counts and tested recovery procedures. This is the strongest reason to use Option B for production.

5.4 Operational feasibility verdict

Feasible for a prototype and demonstration. Not recommended for unattended production use without the monitoring, upgrade tooling, security and operational experience that mature platforms provide.

SOURCE PAGE 9 / 14

Storage sizing formula:

Storage needed = (average message size x messages per second x 86,400 x retention days) x replication factor

Example: 1 KB messages at 1,000 msg/s with 7-day retention and replication factor 3 gives about 1 KB x 1,000 x 86,400 x 7 x 3, which is roughly 1.8 TB across the cluster. This single calculation shows why retention and replication settings dominate cost.

6.4 Benefits

• Tangible: a working reference implementation, a complete design document and

diagrams, measurable benchmarks of partitioning and acks trade-offs. • Intangible: strong understanding of distributed systems, directly applicable when

operating or tuning production platforms, and strong material for interviews and viva examinations.

6.5 Economic feasibility verdict

Feasible. The cash cost of the prototype is negligible, and the return is educational and architectural. For production, the economics favor adopting an existing platform rather than building one.

7. Legal and Compliance Feasibility

7.1 Licensing and intellectual property

• The design uses publicly documented, well-established concepts (append-only logs,

partitioning, replication). Concepts and algorithms are not owned, but source code is. • Do not copy source code from Kafka or other products into the prototype without

respecting their license. Apache Kafka is released under the Apache License 2.0, which permits use with attribution and notices. Cite all references in the report. • Any libraries used should be open source with licenses compatible with the project's

intended distribution. Record each dependency and its license.

7.2 Data protection and privacy

The prototype should use synthetic or anonymized data only. If the design is ever applied to real user data, the following apply:

Mitigation

Concern Why it matters for a commit log

Logs are immutable and replicated, so individual records are hard to delete

Right to erasure and data minimization (for example under GDPR, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023)

Short retention, avoid putting personal data in keys and payloads where possible, store references instead of raw data, use per-user encryption keys that can be destroyed (crypto-shredding), or use compaction with tombstones (future work)

Data localization and cross-border transfer

Replicas may sit in different regions

Keep all replicas within an approved region

Encryption in transit (TLS) and at rest, access control lists (future work)

Confidentiality Anyone with disk or network access could read records

Auditability Regulated sectors need access trails

Log administrative actions and client access

Event payloads may include regulated data

Do not carry regulated data in the prototype. Production use requires a compliance review

Sector rules (for example HIPAA for health data, PCI DSS for payment data)

7.3 Academic integrity

Clearly separate original work from referenced material, cite sources for diagrams and concepts, and state which parts were implemented versus only designed.

7.4 Legal feasibility verdict

No blocking issues for a prototype using synthetic data and open-source tooling. Privacy and security controls must be designed in before any real data is processed.

9. Final Recommendation

9.1 Decision

GO. Proceed with Option C as a phased design-and-prototype project, with Level 1 to 3 as committed scope and Level 4 (replication and failover) as a stretch goal. For any production deployment, adopt an existing platform (Option B) rather than operating the prototype.

9.2 Rationale

1. It satisfies every objective of a system design microproject: a clear problem, a justified

architecture, trade-off analysis and a working demonstration. 2. Technical, economic, schedule and legal feasibility are all positive, with manageable

risks. 3. The phased scope guarantees a complete result even if replication proves harder than

planned. 4. Comparing the prototype against Options A and B shows the reasoning behind real-

world architecture choices.

9.3 Conditions for GO

• Scope frozen at the end of the design phase. • Synthetic data only. • Level 4 clearly marked optional. • Benchmark claims limited to measured results.

Appendix A: Assumptions

• Team of about three students or engineers, part time, over 6 to 8 weeks. • Prototype runs on laptops, optionally on three small cloud virtual machines for a demo. • Synthetic data only. • Cost figures are indicative and must be checked against current provider pricing. • Performance figures will be measured during Phase 6, and none are promised in

advance.

Appendix B: Glossary

Term Meaning

Commit log Append-only, ordered, durable sequence of records

Partition One ordered slice of a topic, the unit of parallelism

Offset A record's position within a partition

Broker Server that stores partitions and serves requests

ISR In-sync replicas: followers caught up with the leader

High watermark Highest offset replicated to all in-sync replicas, the limit for consumer reads

Consumer group Consumers that share a topic's partitions, one consumer per partition

At-least-once No loss, possible duplicates

Idempotent Processing the same message twice has the same effect as once
